{{short description|Relation between density and radius for a white dwarf}}
In [[astrophysics]], '''Chandrasekhar's white dwarf equation''' is an initial value [[ordinary differential equation]] introduced by the [[Indian American]] [[astrophysicist]] [[Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar]],<ref>Chandrasekhar, Subrahmanyan, and Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar. An introduction to the study of stellar structure. Vol. 2. Chapter 11 Courier Corporation, 1958.</ref> in his study of the gravitational potential of completely degenerate [[white dwarf]] stars. The equation reads as<ref>{{cite book|last=Davis|first=Harold Thayer|title=Introduction to Nonlinear Differential and Integral Equations|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RgbWowrjKd4C|year=1962|publisher=Courier Corporation|isbn=978-0-486-60971-3}}</ref>
<math display="block">\frac 1 {\eta^2} \frac d {d\eta}\left(\eta^2 \frac{d\varphi}{d\eta}\right) + (\varphi^2 - C)^{3/2} = 0</math>
with initial conditions
<math display="block">\varphi(0)=1, \quad \varphi'(0)=0</math>
where <math>\varphi</math> measures the density of white dwarf, <math>\eta</math> is the [[dimensionless number|non-dimensional]] radial distance from the center and <math>C</math> is a constant which is related to the density of the white dwarf at the center. The boundary <math>\eta=\eta_\infty</math> of the equation is defined by the condition
<math display="block">\varphi(\eta_\infty) = \sqrt{C}.</math>
such that the range of <math>\varphi</math> becomes <math>\sqrt{C}\leq\varphi\leq 1</math>. This condition is equivalent to saying that the density vanishes at <math>\eta=\eta_\infty</math>.

== Derivation ==
From the quantum statistics of a completely degenerate electron gas (all the lowest quantum states are occupied), the [[pressure]] and the [[density]] of a white dwarf are calculated in terms of the maximum electron momentum <math>p_0</math>standardized as <math>x = p_0 / mc</math>, with pressure <math>P = A f(x)</math> and density <math>\rho = B x^3</math>, where
<math display="block">
\begin{align}
& A = \frac{\pi m_\text{e}^4 c^5}{3h^3} = 6.02\times 10^{21} \text{ Pa}, \\
& B = \frac{8\pi}{3}m_p\mu_\text{e}\left(\frac{m_\text{e} c}{h}\right)^3 = 9.82\times 10^8 \mu_\text{e} \text{ kg/m}^3, \\
& f(x) = x(2x^2-3)(x^2+1)^{1/2} + 3 \sinh^{-1} x,
\end{align}
</math>

<math>\mu_\text{e}</math> is the mean molecular weight of the gas, and <math>h</math> is the [[Planck constant]]. 

When this is substituted into the [[hydrostatic equilibrium]] equation
<math display="block">\frac 1 {r^2} \frac{d}{dr}\left(\frac{r^2}{\rho}\frac{dP}{dr}\right)=-4\pi G \rho</math>
where <math>G</math> is the [[gravitational constant]] and <math>r</math> is the radial distance, we get
<math display="block">\frac{1}{r^2} \frac{d}{dr}\left(r^2\frac{d\sqrt{x^2+1}}{dr}\right)=-\frac{\pi G B^2}{2A}x^3</math>
and letting <math>y^2 = x^2 + 1</math>, we have
<math display="block">\frac{1}{r^2} \frac{d}{dr}\left(r^2\frac{dy}{dr}\right)=-\frac{\pi G B^2}{2A}(y^2-1)^{3/2}</math>

If we denote the density at the origin as <math>\rho_\text{o} = B x_\text{o}^3 = B (y_\text{o}^2-1)^{3/2} </math>, then a non-dimensional scale
<math display="block">r = \left(\frac{2A}{\pi G B^2}\right)^{1/2} \frac{\eta}{y_\text{o}}, \quad y = y_\text{o} \varphi</math>
gives
<math display="block">\frac{1}{\eta^2} \frac{d}{d\eta}\left(\eta^2 \frac{d\varphi}{d\eta}\right) + (\varphi^2 - C)^{3/2} = 0</math>
where <math>C=1/y_\text{o}^2</math>. In other words, once the above equation is solved the density is given by
<math display="block">\rho = B y_\text{o}^3 \left(\varphi^2 - \frac 1 {y_\text{o}^2}\right)^{3/2}.</math>

The mass interior to a specified point can then be calculated
<math display="block">M(\eta) = -\frac{4\pi}{B^2}\left(\frac{2A}{\pi G}\right)^{3/2}\eta^2\frac{d\varphi}{d\eta}.</math>

The radius–mass relation of the white dwarf is usually plotted in the plane <math>\eta_\infty</math>–<math>M(\eta_\infty)</math>.

== Solution near the origin ==

In the neighborhood of the origin, <math>\eta\ll 1</math>, Chandrasekhar provided an [[asymptotic expansion]] as
<math display="block">
\begin{align}
\varphi = {} & 1 - \frac{q^3} 6 \eta^2 + \frac{q^4}{40} \eta^4 - \frac{q^5(5q^2+14)}{7!} \eta^6 \\[6pt]
& {} + \frac{q^6(339q^2 + 280)}{3\times 9!}\eta^8 - \frac{q^7(1425q^4 + 11346q^2 + 4256)}{5\times 11!}\eta^{10} + \cdots
\end{align}
</math>
where <math>q^2 = C-1</math>. He also provided numerical solutions for the range <math>C = 0.01 - 0.8 </math>.

== Equation for small central densities ==

When the central density <math>\rho_\text{o} = B x_\text{o}^3 = B (y_\text{o}^2-1)^{3/2} </math> is small, the equation can be reduced to a [[Lane–Emden equation]] by introducing
<math display="block">\xi = \sqrt{2}\eta, \qquad \theta = \varphi^2-C= \varphi^2-1+x_\text{o}^2 + O(x_\text{o}^4)</math>
to obtain at leading order, the following equation
<math display="block">\frac{1}{\xi^2}\frac{d}{d\xi}\left(\xi^2\frac{d\theta}{d\xi}\right) = - \theta^{3/2}</math>
subjected to the conditions <math>\theta(0)=x_\text{o}^2</math> and <math>\theta'(0)=0</math>. Note that although the equation reduces to the Lane–Emden equation with [[polytrope|polytropic]] index <math>3/2</math>, the [[initial condition]] is not that of the Lane–Emden equation.

== Limiting mass for large central densities ==
When the central density becomes large, i.e., <math>y_\text{o}\rightarrow \infty</math> or equivalently <math>C\rightarrow 0</math>, the governing equation reduces to
<math display="block">\frac{1}{\eta^2}\frac{d}{d\eta}\left(\eta^2\frac{d\varphi}{d\eta}\right) = - \varphi^{3}</math>
subjected to the conditions <math>\varphi(0)=1</math> and <math>\varphi'(0)=0</math>. This is exactly the Lane–Emden equation with polytropic index <math>3</math>. Note that in this limit of large densities, the radius 
<math display="block">r = \left(\frac{2A}{\pi G B^2}\right)^{1/2} \frac{\eta}{y_\text{o}}</math>
tends to zero. The mass of the white dwarf however tends to a finite limit
<math display="block">M\rightarrow - \frac{4\pi}{B^2}\left(\frac{2A}{\pi G}\right)^{3/2}\left(\eta^2 \frac{d\varphi}{d\eta}\right)_{\eta=\eta_\infty}=5.75 \mu_\text{e}^{-2}M_\odot.</math>

The [[Chandrasekhar limit]] follows from this limit.
